United Kingdom.answer: For Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales), GOV.UK says you cannot bring meat, meat products, milk or dairy from outside the EU, with a few exceptions such as up to 2kg of powdered infant milk. From the EU, Switzerland, Norway and a few other places fish, poultry and eggs are allowed but most meat and all dairy are not. Undeclared banned products can mean a fine of up to £5,000 or prosecution.
sources: https://www.gov.uk/bringing-food-into-great-britain
GOV.UK — Bringing food into Great Britain
faq: Can I bring cheese or milk into Great Britain?

GOV.UK says no for dairy such as cheese, milk, butter and yoghurt, from the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein, the Faroe Islands and Greenland as well as from other countries. The exception is up to 2kg of powdered infant milk, infant food or special medical food.
Can I bring meat into Great Britain?
Not from outside the EU. From the EU and the other listed places, pork, beef, lamb, mutton, goat, venison and products made from them, such as sausages, are not allowed, but poultry is.
Can I bring fruit and vegetables into Great Britain?

From the EU, Switzerland or Liechtenstein, yes for personal use. From other countries most need a phytosanitary certificate; without one you can bring only the items GOV.UK lists, such as pineapple, citrus fruit, banana, mango, dates and guava.
What happens if I do not declare banned food?
Border Force destroys declared banned products. If you do not declare them, GOV.UK says you could be fined up to £5,000 (in England) or prosecuted.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: Meat and dairy from outside the EU are banned; from the EU, cheese, milk and most meat are banned too.

lines: You cannot bring meat or meat products, or milk or milk-based products.
Exceptions: up to 2kg per person of powdered infant milk, infant food or special food needed for medical reasons, in branded unopened packaging and not needing refrigeration.

scen.when: From the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein, the Faroe Islands or Greenland
lines: No pork, beef, lamb, mutton, goat, venison or products made from them, such as sausages.
No cheese, milk, butter or yoghurt.
Poultry and its products, and other animal products such as eggs and honey, are allowed for personal use.

topics.label: Fish & seafood
topics.head: From outside the EU you can bring up to 20 kg of fish in total.

lines: Up to 20kg per person in total of fresh fish (gutted), fish products, processed fish (dried, cooked, cured or smoked), lobsters and prawns.
Up to 2kg per person of honey, live mussels or oysters, snails, frogs’ legs and insect protein.
Caviar needs a CITES permit.

topics.label: Fruit, veg & nuts
topics.head: Free from the EU; from elsewhere most need a plant health certificate.

scen.when: From the EU, Switzerland or Liechtenstein
lines: Fruit, vegetables, nuts and seeds are allowed for personal use.
Most fruit and vegetables need a phytosanitary certificate from the authorities of the country you leave.
Without one you may bring only pineapple, kiwi, coconut, citrus fruits, kumquat, persimmon, durian, curry leaves, banana and plantain, mango, dates, passion fruit and guava.
Processed and packaged plant products, peeled and processed nuts or nut butters, and certain grains such as rice are also allowed.

topics.label: Packaged food
topics.head: Bread, biscuits, pasta and similar items can come from any country.

lines: Bread (not sandwiches filled with meat or dairy), cakes without fresh cream, biscuits, chocolate and confectionery (not with a lot of unprocessed dairy), pasta and noodles (not meat-filled), packaged soup, stocks and flavourings.
Processed and packaged plant products, and food supplements with small amounts of an animal product such as fish oil capsules.

topics.label: Pet food
topics.head: Pet food is mostly banned from outside the EU; 2 kg only for health reasons.

scen.when: From the EU and the other listed places
lines: Pet food with pig, cow, sheep, goat or deer meat or animal products is not allowed.
Other pet food, such as chicken, is allowed if commercially packaged with the maker’s name and address, up to 2kg per person.
Not allowed unless your pet needs it for health reasons, then up to 2kg per person, unopened and branded, not needing refrigeration.
Your pet must travel with you and you should carry evidence such as a vet’s letter. For more than 2kg, email imports@apha.gov.uk.

topics.label: If you break the rules
topics.head: Banned items are destroyed; undeclared ones can mean a fine of up to £5,000.

lines: Declared banned products are taken away and destroyed by Border Force.
If you do not declare them, you could be fined up to £5,000 (in England) or prosecuted.
Border Force can also seize products that are cross-contaminated, for example with meat blood; contaminated clothing or bags are destroyed. You can appeal if you think products were wrongly seized.
Northern Ireland has different rules, which this page does not cover.

Canada.answer: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency says you must declare all food products you bring into Canada, and most foods are capped at 20 kg (or 20 L for liquids) for personal use. Rules differ by origin: meat from the US is allowed if retail packaged, while from other countries only commercially prepared, cooked, shelf-stable meat in sealed containers is allowed. Eggs from outside the US are not permitted.
sources: https://inspection.canada.ca/en/food-safety-consumers/bring-food-personal-use
Canadian Food Inspection Agency — Bring food into Canada for personal use
faq: Do I have to declare food when entering Canada?
Yes. The CFIA says that when travelling you must declare all food products you bring with you, and the Canada Border Services Agency may inspect them at the point of entry.
How much food can I bring into Canada?

For personal use only, with caps such as 20 kg for meat, dairy, fruit and vegetables, 5 dozen eggs from the US, 50 L of non-alcoholic drinks and 50 L of food-grade oils. Most other foods are capped at 20 kg, or 20 L for liquids.
Can I bring meat into Canada?

From the US, retail packaged or labelled meat with proof of origin, up to 20 kg. From other countries, fresh, dried and cured meats such as ham and sausage are not permitted; only commercially prepared, cooked, shelf-stable products in sealed containers, up to 20 kg.
Can I bring eggs into Canada?
Retail-packaged eggs labelled Product of the USA, up to 5 dozen, from the US. Eggs from other countries are not permitted.

topics.label: Meat
topics.head: From the US retail-packaged meat is allowed; from elsewhere only cooked, sealed products.

lines: Only if you bring it with you, not by mail or courier, retail packaged or labelled, with proof of country of origin.
Farm or backyard meat that is not retail packaged is not permitted. Limit: 20 kg (44.09 lbs).
Fresh, dried and cured meats such as hams and sausages are not permitted.
Only commercially prepared, cooked, shelf-stable products in sealed containers, brought with you, up to 20 kg. Beef only from countries of negligible BSE risk.

topics.label: Dairy
topics.head: Up to 20 kg or 20 L; from outside the US only certain dairy products.

lines: No specific restrictions are listed for cheese, yogurt, butter, milk, ice cream and kashk.
Limit: 20 kg (44.09 lbs) or 20 L (5.28 US gal).
Only ice cream, yogurt, kashk and pasteurized cheese are permitted from any country.
Unpasteurized cheese only from countries free of certain animal diseases. Limit 20 kg or 20 L.

topics.label: Eggs
topics.head: Retail-packaged eggs from the US only, up to 5 dozen.

lines: Must be retail packaged, for human consumption, and labelled Product of the USA. Farm or backyard eggs are not permitted.
Processed egg products: up to 20 kg or 20 L.
Eggs are not permitted.

topics.label: Fruit & veg
topics.head: Up to 20 kg each; fresh produce from outside the US may be restricted.

lines: Fresh produce is subject to the Automated Import Reference System (AIRS).
Potatoes must be commercially packaged and graded US No.1. Limits: fruits 20 kg, vegetables 20 kg.
Fresh produce is subject to AIRS and may be restricted or prohibited depending on the country of origin; if permitted, 20 kg of fruit and 20 kg of vegetables.
Processed produce: 20 kg or 20 L.

topics.label: Drinks, oils & others
topics.head: Most other foods are fine within the quantity caps.

lines: Non-alcoholic beverages 50 L, food-grade oils 50 L, maple syrup 20 L, maple products 4 kg.
Most other foods, such as baked goods, confectionery, honey, spices, tea, coffee and grain foods: 20 kg, or 20 L for liquids.
Duties and taxes may apply above the personal exemption limits.
Alcohol and tobacco follow Canada Border Services Agency limits, which this page links to.

Japan.answer: Japan's Animal Quarantine Service requires every traveller bringing in meat, organs, eggs or processed products such as jerky, ham, sausages and bacon to be inspected at the counter in the baggage claim area, and these items need a government inspection certificate from the exporting country. Without one they cannot enter, even as souvenirs. Bringing them in illegally is punishable by up to 3 years in prison or a fine of up to 3 million yen.
sources: https://www.maff.go.jp/aqs/english/product/import.html
MAFF Animal Quarantine Service — importing animal products
faq: Can I bring meat or sausages into Japan?

Meat, organs and processed products such as jerky, ham, sausages and bacon need a government-issued inspection certificate from the exporting country. Without one they cannot be brought in, even as souvenirs or for personal use.
Can I bring eggs into Japan?
Eggs, including eggshells, are subject to animal quarantine and need the same inspection certificate.
Do I have to go through inspection when I arrive in Japan?
Yes: travellers must undergo import inspection at the Animal Quarantine Service counter in the baggage claim area of the arrival airport or seaport.
What is the penalty for bringing animal products into Japan illegally?
A custodial sentence of up to 3 years or a fine of up to 3 million yen (up to 50 million yen for businesses). The fine maximum was raised from 1 million yen on 1 July 2020.

topics.label: Meat & sausage
topics.head: Meat and processed meat need a government certificate from the exporting country.

lines: Meat, organs, eggs (including eggshells) and processed products are subject to quarantine. Examples named: jerky, ham, sausages, bacon and meat buns.
Items need a government-issued inspection certificate from the exporting country; without one they cannot be brought in, even as souvenirs or for personal use.
Vacuum-sealed, heat-processed, duty-free and small personal quantities are still not allowed if they are banned or lack a certificate.

topics.label: Eggs
topics.head: Eggs, shells included, are subject to animal quarantine.

lines: Eggs, including eggshells, need the same government inspection certificate.
Items from countries or regions with suspended imports cannot be brought in.

topics.label: Dried fish
topics.head: Dried fish without livestock meat or eggs is not subject to inspection.

lines: Dried fish without livestock meat or eggs is not subject to inspection, but an officer may check it on arrival.

topics.label: Fruit & veg
topics.head: The page states fruits and vegetables are illegal to bring in.

lines: The animal quarantine page states that bringing in fruits, vegetables and similar items is illegal, and links to a separate plant quarantine page that we did not read.
Check the plant protection pages of MAFF before you travel with any plant product.

topics.label: Inspection & fines
topics.head: You are inspected at the Animal Quarantine counter; breaking the rules can mean prison.

lines: Travellers must undergo import inspection at the Animal Quarantine Service counter in the baggage claim area, and officers can ask whether you carry animal products and inspect your luggage.
Bringing in meat or animal products illegally is punishable by a custodial sentence of up to 3 years or a fine of up to 3 million yen.
Failing to declare meat or animal products found in your luggage is also punishable, and officers may dispose of them.

United States.answer: USDA APHIS says every traveller entering the United States must declare all agricultural and wildlife products to U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and that if you declare everything you face no penalties even when an item cannot enter. Almost all fresh and frozen fruits and vegetables are prohibited, meat depends on the animal diseases in the country it comes from (50 pounds is the limit per item), and butter and solid cheeses may enter from any country.
sources: https://www.aphis.usda.gov/traveling-with-ag-products/another-country
USDA APHIS — Traveling from another country with food or agricultural products
https://www.aphis.usda.gov/traveling-with-ag-products/fruits-vegetables
USDA APHIS — International traveler: fruits and vegetables
https://www.aphis.usda.gov/traveling-with-ag-products/milk-dairy-eggs
USDA APHIS — International traveler: milk, dairy and egg products
faq: Do I have to declare food when entering the United States?

Yes. APHIS says travellers must declare all agricultural or wildlife products to CBP, and must also say if they visited a farm or touched animals before the trip. As long as you declare everything you will not face any penalties, even if an inspector decides an item cannot enter.
Can I bring fresh fruit and vegetables into the United States?

Almost all fresh and frozen fruits and vegetables, whole or cut, are prohibited, including ones given to you on a plane or cruise ship. Commercially canned ones are allowed if declared; home-canned products are not.
Can I bring cheese and butter into the United States?
Butter, butter oil and solid hard or soft cheeses may enter from any country if the cheese has no meat and does not pour like a liquid, such as ricotta or cottage cheese.
How much meat can I bring into the United States?

From countries without certain livestock diseases, with proof of origin, no more than 50 pounds of an item. Cured hams and salami from France, Germany, Italy and Spain may not be brought in by travellers.

topics.label: Declare it
topics.head: Declare all agricultural products; declared items bring no penalty even if refused.

lines: Travellers must declare all agricultural and wildlife products to CBP, and tell them if they visited a farm or were in contact with animals.
Inspectors have the final say. Keep receipts and original packaging as proof of the country of origin.
As long as you declare everything you will not face any penalties, even if an inspector decides the items cannot enter.

topics.label: Fruit & veg
topics.head: Almost all fresh and frozen fruit and vegetables are prohibited.

lines: Almost all fresh and frozen fruits and vegetables, whole or cut, are prohibited, including those given to you on an airplane or cruise ship. Plan to leave them behind.
Commercially canned fruit and vegetables are allowed if declared on your customs form; home-canned products are not.
Most dried fruit and vegetables are not allowed. Generally allowed if declared: beans, dates, figs, nuts (not chestnuts or acorns), okra, peas, raisins and Szechwan peppercorns.

topics.label: Meat & poultry
topics.head: Allowed from disease-free countries with proof of origin, up to 50 pounds of an item.

lines: Most is not allowed from countries with foot-and-mouth disease, BSE, swine vesicular disease, classical swine fever or African swine fever.
From countries without these diseases, fresh, cooked, cured or dried meat is allowed with proof of origin such as a label, receipt, passport or flight origin. Not more than 50 pounds of an item.
Cured hams (prosciutto, Serrano, Iberian) and salami from France, Germany, Italy and Spain may not be brought in by travellers.
Most poultry is not allowed from countries with highly pathogenic avian influenza or Newcastle disease.
Commercially packaged, cooked, shelf-stable poultry in unopened packages from affected countries is allowed, up to 50 pounds per item.

topics.label: Dairy & eggs
topics.head: Butter and solid cheeses are allowed from any country; other dairy and eggs depend on origin.

lines: Most milk and dairy from countries with foot-and-mouth disease is not allowed, except small quantities of infant liquid milk and formula, and commercially packaged, cooked, shelf-stable finished foods.
Butter, butter oil and solid hard or soft cheese (no meat, and not pourable like ricotta) may enter from any country.
Most eggs and egg products from countries with avian influenza or Newcastle disease are not allowed.
From other countries, eggs are allowed with proof of origin. Clean decorated eggshells without egg white or yolk: up to 12 per person.

topics.label: Seafood
topics.head: APHIS does not regulate most seafood; other agencies do.

lines: APHIS only regulates breaded seafood whose breading contains milk or eggs.
For other seafood contact the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service or the Food and Drug Administration, whose numbers are on the page.

New Zealand.answer: The Ministry for Primary Industries says you must declare all food, animal products, plants and other risk goods on your New Zealand Traveller Declaration, and that any food, cooked, uncooked, fresh, preserved, packaged or dried, counts as a risk good. Failing to declare is a strict liability offence with a NZD$400 instant fine, and deliberate smuggling can mean up to NZD$100,000 and 5 years in prison.
sources: https://www.mpi.govt.nz/bring-send-to-nz/bringing-and-posting-items-to-nz/how-to-declare-items-when-arriving-in-nz/
Ministry for Primary Industries — How to declare items when arriving in NZ
https://www.mpi.govt.nz/bring-send-to-nz/bringing-and-posting-items-to-nz/what-happens-if-you-fail-to-declare
Ministry for Primary Industries — What happens if you fail to declare
faq: Do I have to declare all food in New Zealand?

Yes. MPI says to declare all food, animal products, plants and other specific items on your New Zealand Traveller Declaration (NZTD), free online or in the app. It counts any food, cooked, uncooked, fresh, preserved, packaged or dried, as a risk good.
What if I forget to declare something?
It is still an offence. MPI calls it a strict liability offence, even if you forgot or did not know the rules. The penalty is a NZD$400 infringement fee, with no criminal conviction.
What is the penalty for deliberate smuggling?
If you are convicted of deliberate smuggling you could be fined up to NZD$100,000 and sentenced to up to 5 years in prison.
Can I throw food away instead of declaring it?
MPI says you can dispose of undeclared risk goods in the marked amnesty bins on arrival, to avoid being searched or fined.

topics.label: Declare it
topics.head: Declare all food and animal or plant products; there is no excuse for forgetting.

scen.when: On the New Zealand Traveller Declaration
lines: Declare all risk goods like food, plants, wooden products, soil, water, outdoor equipment and animal products, even if you have nothing in your bags to declare you must still complete the declaration.
Declared items may be inspected. Dispose of undeclared risk goods in the marked amnesty bins on arrival to avoid being searched or fined.

topics.label: Any food
topics.head: MPI treats any food, cooked, fresh, packaged or dried, as a risk good.

lines: Any food: cooked, uncooked, fresh, preserved, packaged or dried.
Animals or animal products: meat, dairy products, fish, honey, bee products, eggs, feathers, shells, raw wool, skins, bones or insects.
Plants or plant products: fruit, flowers, seeds, bulbs, wood, bark, leaves, nuts, vegetables, fungi, cane, bamboo or straw, including for religious offerings or medicinal use.
MPI says it cannot list every risk good, because risk depends on the country, ingredients and packaging.
Use its Check if you can bring or send an item to NZ tool for specific foods and weight limits; we did not read that tool.

topics.label: Outdoor gear
topics.head: Items used outdoors or on farms must be declared too.

lines: Equipment used with animals, plants or water, and items used for outdoor or farming activities, including footwear, tents, camping, hunting, hiking, golf or sports equipment.
Other risk items include animal medicines, herbal medicines, biological cultures, organisms, soil and water.

topics.label: Fines
topics.head: Forgetting is no excuse: NZD$400 instant fine, up to NZD$100,000 for smuggling.

lines: The penalty for a false declaration is an NZD$400 infringement fee, an instant fine, with no criminal conviction. It applies even if you forgot, were careless or did not know the rules or what was in your baggage.
You can pay within 14 days, ask for a waiver, or request a court hearing.
If you deliberately make an incorrect or false declaration to conceal items and are convicted of smuggling, you could be fined up to NZD$100,000 and sentenced to up to 5 years in prison.

Australia.answer: Australia's Department of Agriculture says that by law you must declare if you are carrying certain food, plant material or animal products when you travel to Australia, and that goods are assessed by a biosecurity officer and may be inspected. Its list of foods to check covers items such as meat, dairy, eggs, rice, honey, nuts and fruit preserves, with detailed conditions in its BICON system. Footwear, clothing and equipment used in rural areas must be cleaned and declared.
sources: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/travelling/bringing-mailing-goods
Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Bringing or mailing goods to Australia
faq: Do I have to declare food when I arrive in Australia?

Yes. The department says that by law you must declare if you are carrying certain food, plant material or animal products. You can take declared goods to the clearance point for assessment, or voluntarily dispose of them in the terminal bins.
Where do I find the detailed rules for each food in Australia?

In the department's Biosecurity Import Conditions system (BICON). Its food and drink list covers items such as meat, cheese and dairy, eggs, honey, rice, nuts, noodles, spices, pet food and infant formula, but it says the list is not exhaustive.
What if my shoes or equipment were used on a farm?
All footwear, clothing and equipment used in rural areas or near animals must be thoroughly cleaned and declared on arrival.
What happens to goods that do not meet the import conditions?
They will be directed for treatment or exported at the importer's expense, or the traveller can voluntarily dispose of them.

topics.label: Declare it
topics.head: You must declare certain food, plant material and animal products.

lines: By law you must declare if you are carrying certain food, plant material or animal products.
You can take declared goods to the clearance point, where a biosecurity officer assesses them and they may be inspected. Or you can voluntarily dispose of them in the bins in the terminal.

topics.label: Food on the list
topics.head: The department lists food types to check before you travel.

lines: Biscuits, bread, cakes and pastries; cheese, butter and dairy; chocolate; coffee; fish; honey; infant formula; juice; meat items; noodles and pasta; nuts; oil; preserved fruit and vegetables; rice; sauces; seafood; spices; tea; wheat; whole eggs and more.
The page says the list is not exhaustive, and the conditions for each item are in the Biosecurity Import Conditions system (BICON), which we did not read.

topics.label: Farm items
topics.head: Footwear, clothing and equipment used on farms must be cleaned and declared.

lines: All footwear, clothing and equipment used in rural areas or near animals must be thoroughly cleaned and declared on arrival.

topics.label: Mail & rejected goods
topics.head: Mailed goods must be described accurately; goods that fail conditions are treated or exported.

scen.when: Goods that do not meet the conditions
lines: Goods that do not meet import conditions will be directed for treatment or exported at the importer’s expense, or you can voluntarily dispose of them.
Goods sent by mail must be accurately described on the postal declaration label.
We did not read the penalty amounts for failing to declare; check the department’s page on penalties before you travel.

Hong Kong.answer: Hong Kong's Imported Game, Meat, Poultry and Eggs Regulations require every consignment of game, meat, poultry and eggs, whether for personal use or not, to carry a health certificate or written permission from the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department. Breaking the rule is punishable by a fine of HK$50,000 and 6 months in prison, and the Centre for Food Safety had brought 774 prosecutions against inbound travellers by 20 June 2024.
sources: https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202406/21/P2024062100547.htm
Hong Kong Government (Customs and Centre for Food Safety) — joint operation against illegal import of regulated food
faq: Can I bring meat, poultry or eggs into Hong Kong?
Only with a health certificate from the place of origin or written permission from the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department. The law applies whether the food is for personal use or not.
What is the penalty for bringing regulated food into Hong Kong illegally?
On conviction, a maximum fine of HK$50,000 and six months' imprisonment under Cap. 132AK.
Does food from the Mainland need papers?
Yes: food from the Mainland needs a health certificate from Mainland Customs showing it comes from a registered plant recognised by the Mainland authority.
How common are prosecutions?
The Centre for Food Safety had brought 774 prosecutions against inbound persons for illegally bringing game, meat, poultry and eggs by 20 June 2024.

topics.label: Meat, poultry, game
topics.head: Every consignment needs a health certificate or written permission, even for personal use.

lines: Each consignment must be accompanied by a health certificate from the issuing entity of the place of origin, or by written permission from the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD).

The rule applies whether the food is for personal use or not. Food from the Mainland needs a health certificate from Mainland Customs showing it is from a registered plant recognised for supplying Hong Kong.

topics.label: Eggs
topics.head: Eggs are regulated food with the same health certificate rule.

lines: The release names raw meat, poultry and eggs as its examples of illegal imports of regulated food.
Importing regulated food needs a recognised health certificate, FEHD written permission, or an import licence.

topics.label: Penalty
topics.head: A fine of HK$50,000 and six months in prison on conviction.

lines: Maximum penalty on conviction is a fine of $50,000 and six months’ imprisonment under Cap. 132AK.

Between 18 and 21 June 2024 a joint operation at Lo Wu, Lok Ma Chau Spur Line, Shenzhen Bay and Heung Yuen Wai found 15 cases; by 20 June the Centre for Food Safety had instituted 774 prosecutions that year.
The public can report suspected smuggling to the Customs 24-hour hotline, 2545 6182, or to crimereport@customs.gov.hk.

topics.label: Not read
topics.head: The release does not list other foods such as fruit or dairy.

lines: This government release covers regulated food: game, meat, poultry and eggs. It does not list rules for fruit, vegetables, dairy or packaged food, so check the Centre for Food Safety (cfs.gov.hk) before you bring them.
